question: Are NYC's streets more dangerous at night? Make a chart and give a conclusion for a news report.

options.metric: Annual share of recorded crashes by time-of-day group
options.denominator: All recorded crash rows in that calendar year
options.grouping: Calendar year and night (20:00–23:59 and 00:01–05:59), day (06:00–19:59), or midnight/unknown (00:00 or missing time)
options.reason: A news report may want to describe when recorded crashes occur, while keeping frequency distinct from injury severity.
options.answer: This file cannot establish whether NYC streets are more dangerous at night; in 2025, 27.95% of recorded crashes were at night, 70.01% by day, and 2.04% had midnight or unknown times.
options.interpretation: The file only partly answers the question: this line chart shows each year's share of all police-reported NYC motor-vehicle crashes in complete calendar years 2013–2025, defining night as 20:00–23:59 and 00:01–05:59, day as 06:00–19:59, and midnight or missing times as ambiguous/unclassified. In 2025, 27.95% of 85,546 crash rows were night, 70.01% day, and 2.04% ambiguous; this is a defensible measure of recorded crash frequency by clock time, not severity. It leaves risk per trip or hour of travel unanswered because the file contains no traffic-volume or travel-exposure denominator. The check excludes partial 2012 (100,545 rows) and 2026 (36,424 rows), finds no NULL times in 2013–2025 but 23,787 midnight-coded rows that are shown separately because the annual count jumps from 24 in 2015 to 2,895 in 2016, and the largest neighboring all-row denominator change is a 98,568-row drop from 2019 (211,486) to 2020 (112,918), so a change in share across those years can reflect the changed row denominator/composition rather than a change in an underlying outcome and warrants caution.

options.metric: Annual mean recorded persons injured plus killed per eligible crash, by time of day
options.denominator: Eligible crash rows with nonmissing, non-midnight crash_time and nonmissing number_of_persons_injured and number_of_persons_killed
options.grouping: Calendar year and night (20:00–23:59 and 00:01–05:59) or day (06:00–19:59)
options.reason: A per-crash casualty average directly compares recorded crash severity between nighttime and daytime crashes.
options.answer: This file cannot establish exposure-adjusted danger; among eligible crashes in 2025, the mean was 0.602 recorded people injured or killed per night crash versus 0.576 per day crash.
options.interpretation: The file only partly answers the question: this chart plots the annual mean of recorded persons injured plus killed per eligible police-reported NYC crash in complete years 2013–2025, with night defined as 20:00–23:59 and 00:01–05:59 and day as 06:00–19:59. In 2025, the mean was 0.602 casualties per night crash and 0.576 per day crash, making per-crash casualty severity a defensible measure of one part of danger. The data cannot show risk per trip or hour of travel because it has no traffic-exposure denominator. The check excludes partial 2012 (100,545 rows) and 2026 (36,424 rows), 23,787 midnight-coded rows because their count jumps from 24 in 2015 to 2,895 in 2016 and they may be default-coded, and rows missing casualty totals (18 missing injury values and 36 missing death values, with overlap possible); no NULL times were found. Eligible row denominators fall by 97,265 from 208,341 in 2019 to 111,076 in 2020, so a change in the average across those years can reflect a change in the size or composition of the crash denominator and not only casualty outcomes, and should be compared with that caution.

options.metric: Annual percentage of eligible crashes with at least one person killed, by time of day
options.denominator: Eligible crash rows with nonmissing, non-midnight crash_time and nonmissing number_of_persons_killed
options.grouping: Calendar year and night (20:00–23:59 and 00:01–05:59) or day (06:00–19:59)
options.reason: A fatal-crash share highlights the most severe recorded outcome rather than combining deaths with nonfatal injuries.
options.answer: This file cannot establish exposure-adjusted danger; in 2025, 0.422% of eligible night crashes involved a death, compared with 0.192% of eligible day crashes.
options.interpretation: The file only partly answers the question: the chart shows annual shares of eligible police-reported NYC motor-vehicle crashes with at least one person killed in complete years 2013–2025, defining night as 20:00–23:59 and 00:01–05:59 and day as 06:00–19:59. In 2025, the fatal-crash share was 0.422% at night and 0.192% by day, a focused comparison of the most severe recorded crash outcome. It leaves risk per trip or hour of travel unanswered because the data has no traffic-volume or travel-exposure denominator. The check excludes partial 2012 (100,545 rows) and 2026 (36,424 rows), 23,787 midnight-coded rows because of the sharp increase from 24 in 2015 to 2,895 in 2016 and possible default coding, and 36 rows with missing person-killed totals (which may overlap the midnight group); no NULL times were found. The eligible row denominator drops 97,265 from 208,341 in 2019 to 111,076 in 2020, so a change in fatal-crash share across those years can come from a change in the denominator/composition and not the fatal outcome alone, and should be compared with caution.

answer:
1. The crash records cannot establish whether NYC streets are more dangerous at night; in 2025, 27.95% of recorded crashes were at night, 70.01% by day, and 2.04% had midnight or unknown times.
2. The data cannot establish exposure-adjusted danger; among eligible crashes in 2025, the average was 0.602 people injured or killed per night crash versus 0.576 per day crash.
3. The data cannot establish exposure-adjusted danger; in 2025, 0.422% of eligible night crashes involved a death, compared with 0.192% of eligible day crashes.
